full_judgment:
Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury, J : By an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution, the petitioner has called in question the legality of Rules 3(2) and 3(3) of the Land Appeal Board Rules, 1990 as being contrary to section 2 read with section 4 of the Land Appeal Board Act, 1989 and therefore ultra vires to the Constitution. At the same time, the petitioner has also challenged the legality of the order dated 24- 4-2016 passed by the Full Board of the Land Appeal Board, Dhaka in Case No. 4-02/2016 (Bando:), rejecting the case filed by the petitioner and affirming the order dated 6-1-2016 passed by the Member, Land Appeal Board, Dhaka in Case No. 4-02/2016 (Bando:). 

 3. Facts relating to issuance of the Rule are that the petitioner obtained settlement of the land in question on 14-8-2001 in VP Lease Case No. 51, 52, 53, 63, 64/74-75. Challenging the order dated 14-8-2001, respondent No. 10 filed VP Miscellaneous Appeal No. 40 of 2001 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Satkhira, which was dismissed by order dated 14-7-2011 Thereafter, respondent No. 10 filed an appeal before the Additional Divisional Commissioner (Revenue), Khulna (respondent No. 5), being Miscellaneous Case No. 29 of 2015. By order dated 9-2-2015, the operation of the order dated 14-7-2011 passed by respondent No. 7 was stayed Subsequently, respondent No. 9 granted settlement of the land in question in favour of the petitioner. 

 4. Being aggrieved thereby, respondent No. 10 filed an appeal before the Land Appeal Board, Dhaka being Case No. 4-02/2016 (Bando:); Appeal, Satkhira, which was disposed of with certain observation by the Member of the Land Appeal Board by order dated 6-1-2016. Challenging the order dated 6-1-2016, the petitioner preferred an appeal being Case No. 4-20/2016 (Bando:) in — Appeal, Satkhira, which was, however, rejected by the Board. Hence the instant writ petition. 

 5. Mr Md Humayun Kabir, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule submits that the impugned order that was passed by the Full Board of the Land Appeal Board, Dhaka is without lawful authority as the same was passed in violation of the Land Appeal Board Act. He submits that as per the Act, although an appeal is to be decided by the Board comprising of the Chairman and two Members, in the instant case, the impugned decision was passed by a single Member acting as the Full Board. Mr Kabir submits that the impugned order is also not tenable in law as the concerned Member, who passed the impugned order, had earlier passed the order against which the appeal in question was filed by the petitioner. Mr Kabir submits that in gross violation of the well settled principle of law that a person cannot be the Judge of his own decision, the impugned order was passed by the concerned Member of the Board. 

 7. Mr Kabir further submits that there is another practical difficulty in that although the Act provides for a Board to be comprised of three Members, the Rules provide that the Full Board can be constituted by a single Member. He submits that when an appeal from the Board is made to the higher Authority, it is the settled principle of law that the same person cannot sit in both the forums. However, in the instant case, the Member, who had passed the order in the Appeal, himself acted as the Full Board and passed the impugned order. In course of his submission, Mr Kabir has referred to a number of decisions, to which we shall advert in due course. 

 10. Replying to the submission of Mr Kabir on the issue that the same person cannot be judge of the own action, the learned DAG submits that although the appeal was passed by a particular Member of the Board, who also sat on the Appeal Board, the Board was comprised of two other Members and therefore, there was no reason for the petitioner to be aggrieved. He submits that the formation of the Full Board has been done in accordance with law and therefore there is no reason to declare the same as ultra vires to the parent Act. He submits that the Rule itself is misconceived' and therefore it is liable to be discharged. In support of his, contention, the learned DAG has referred to two decisions reported in 10 ADC 148 and 6 BLC 436. 

 17. In most cases, when Parliament passes an Act, a provision is incorporated in the Act, granting power to frame Rules, which may be necessary in future for proper implementation of the particular Act. It is in consonance with such a Parliamentary practice that the. Act of 1990 also provided for framing Of Rules. However those Rules have to be framed for supplication or implementation of the parent Act. The Rules framed under an Act certainly cannot make substantive provisions, like formation of a Full Board, which is not provided in the parent Act. 

 18. In the instant case, the parent Act provides for formation of a Board, which has also been defined in the Act. It is clear that the Act provides for a Board to be comprised of three Members namely, the Chairman and two other Members. However, in clear derogation of the said mandate of the Act, the Rules provide for formation of a Full Board by a single Member. 

 20. In the case of SM Abdur Rouf vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, reported in 66 DLR 308, a similar issue came up for consideration before a Division Bench of this Court. While making the Rule absolute, the Court held as under: 

 "So it is overwhelmingly clear that the appeal the petitioner preferred could only be heard and adjudicated upon by the Land Appeal Board, which, according to section 2, read with section 4 of the Land Appeal Board Act 1989, is composed of the chair thereof, plus, no less than two other members. So, the purported initial decision, taken by a single member, was in coram non-judice, as he, on his own, not being the Full Board, was incompetent to dispose of the appeal. The fact that the initial appeal was heard by an incompetent person, necessarily follows that there could, in law, be no review, simply because, review presupposes review of an earlier decision taken by a properly constituted body, the Board in the instant case. In so far as the original appeal was purportedly heard in coram non-judice, considering the subsequent application as a review petition was void equally well." 

 22. As the present case before us involves a similar question of law and facts, we find no reason to disagree with the decisions passed in the aforesaid two cases by the High Court Division. It is also to be noted that neither of the two decisions, referred to above, have been overruled by the Appellate Division. 

 23. This brings us now to the first part of the Rule whereby the vires of sections 3(2) and 3(3) Rules of 1990 has been challenged. It has already been settled by the Appellate Division that where a writ petition can be decided on merit without striking down the law, it is preferable to do so. However, being mindful of the dictum of the Appellate Division and in expressing our total and respectful agreement with the same, we hasten to add that in the instant case, we do not wish to stop at this stage. Let me elaborate. 

 24. The decisions which have been referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner from the High Court Division were both passed in the year 2011 and 2015. In both those decisions, it has been clearly laid down by this Division that a single Member of the Board cannot act as a Full Board and accordingly, the impugned decisions were set-aside (coram non-judice). However, in the instant case, in the impugned order was passed in April, 2016, i.e., after the pronouncement of the judgments in the aforesaid two cases, thereby indicating that the Board was either oblivious or had deliberately acted in violation of the judicial pronouncement made by the highest Court of the land. On both counts, such conduct of the Board can never be condoned; rather, the same is deprecated in no uncertain terms. 

 26. We are fortified in our view by the decision of the Apex Court passed in Anti-Corruption Commission vs Md Bayazid and others, reported in 65 DLR (AD) 97. In that case, the Apex Court held as under : 

 27. In the case of Tahmina Akter Mollah vs Bangladesh, reported in 23 BLC 155, the Court observed as under: 

 28. The learned DAG, in course of his submission, referred to the decisions reported in 6 BLC 436 and 10 ADC (2013) 148. The learned DAG submits that it has been decided in the latter case by the Appellate Division that the Rules framed under the parent Act are to be followed. We do not, for a moment, disagree with the proposition. However, it has to be borne in mind that the very same Apex Court has also pronounced categorically to the effect that when the Rules are in conflict with and/or in consistent with the parent Act, they are liable to be struck down. 

 29. In the instant case, Rule 3(2) and Rule 3(3) of the Rules of 1990 are not only in derogation of the parent Act, they also stand contrary to the provisions of the parent Act.
